why_math: It works because you can keep important past knowledge separate from new knowledge by replaying examples, and you can update carefully by checking that old users still stay satisfied.

math_plain: Train a language model to choose the right tool by starting with easy tool-choices first, then harder ones, while down-weighting bad training examples.
why_math: It works because easier tasks build foundational understanding that helps with harder tasks, and discarding noisy training examples prevents learning false patterns that lead to wrong choices.

math_plain: Find new social events by treating similar images and text as close neighbors, learning which ones belong together without any labeled event names.
why_math: It works because if you arrange multimodal data so similar ones sit near each other in a space, finding groups becomes finding clusters of nearby points; cross-modal alignment lets you compare images and text fairly.

math_plain: Predict which users will buy during sales by learning stable patterns from past data, then using different expert models to adapt for each sale season.
why_math: It works because user behavior has both unchanging patterns and sale-specific shifts; separating stable from temporary patterns lets you reuse past knowledge while adapting to new seasons.

math_plain: Rank items to recommend by focusing on finding new items that previous models missed, avoiding recommending the same things twice.
why_math: It works because if multiple models already retrieved some items, recommending those again wastes ranking power; focusing on truly new items makes each model's contribution distinct and valuable.

math_plain: Learn item descriptions as feature vectors by separating words that matter for one domain from words shared across domains, preventing confusion between domains.
why_math: It works because mixing domain-specific and domain-shared meanings leads to negative transfer; by explicitly separating these, you avoid applying rules learned in one domain wrongly to another.

math_plain: Rank nodes by importance using random walks that approximate a weighted path count, averaging many random samples to speed up the calculation.
why_math: It works because random walks converge to true importance scores given enough samples, and averaging many cheap samples is faster than exact calculation; you get ranking order right even if magnitudes are approximate.

math_plain: Rank items on complex 2D search layouts by learning which combinations of position and item features lead to long-term user satisfaction, not just clicks.
why_math: It works because causal frameworks separate correlation from actual influence; by using quasi-experiments, you avoid false signals like confounding that short-term clicks might hide.

math_plain: Predict what users will want next by remembering only the most important categories from their long history instead of every past click.
why_math: It works because categories already aggregate similar items; throwing away redundant history details keeps only the signal, so the model trains faster and focuses on what matters.

math_plain: Estimate individual treatment effects on a network by learning three types of hidden factors: which help assign treatment, which confuse treatment with outcome, and which adjust for networks.
why_math: It works because treatment effects are biased by confounders and spillover; separating hidden factors lets you identify which are true confounders versus which are just network side effects.

why_math: It works because focusing training on one target feature avoids diluting error signals across many unrelated features; neighbors with similar patterns provide relevant context without adding noise.

math_plain: Extract entities and events from text without seeing the specific schema by first finding spans and assigning concepts, then separately aligning concepts to different schemas.
why_math: It works because general understanding (finding spans) is separate from schema-specific mapping; by splitting these tasks, each one uses only the knowledge it needs, avoiding conflicting pressures.

math_plain: Label new text for named entities by training on confidence scores from a language model, combined with calibration adjustments, to find high-quality pseudo-labels.
why_math: It works because language models have rich knowledge that can judge whether labels are trustworthy; combining confidence with calibration reduces both false certainty and random hallucinations.

math_plain: Decompose matrices by peeling off rank-1 slices using a language model to generate decompositions and a vision model to approve them, without preset stopping thresholds.
why_math: It works because vision models can recognize when remaining structure is noise versus signal better than fixed thresholds; by using learned judgment instead of thresholds, you adapt to the data's inherent rank.
